transitionOut.text: Next: David's Jerusalem, his wars and heirs, Solomon's temple and gates, and the split into Israel and Judah. Tradition and archaeology are told side by side, and where scholars disagree, each view is given.

events.title: The six-chambered gates
events.text: The Bible says Solomon built Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. In the 1950s Yigael Yadin found city gates of the same plan at all three, each with six chambers, and called them Solomon's gates. Israel Finkelstein later moved them about a century down, to the kings of the northern kingdom. At Gezer, radiocarbon dates published in 2023 put the level with the gate back in the 10th century BC.
events.why: Was Solomon a great builder, as the Bible says? The gates are one of the main tests. They show planned building in these years, but not who ordered it, and Hazor and Megiddo are still argued over.
claims: 'Solomon built Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer' (1 Kings 9:15).
Yadin identified the six-chambered gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer as Solomonic.
Finkelstein's 'low chronology' dates these levels to the 9th century BC.

Radiocarbon dates for Gezer Stratum 8, with the gate: built c. 998–957 BC, destroyed c. 969–940 BC (68% ranges). Similar gates are also found elsewhere, so the plan alone does not prove a single builder.

events.title: The copper of Edom
events.text: After Egypt left Canaan, copper smelting in the Arabah valley did not stop. At Khirbet en-Nahas in Faynan and at Timna, huge slag heaps and radiocarbon dates show production on a large scale in the 11th to 9th centuries BC, run by people who mostly lived in tents.
events.why: Archaeologists look for stone palaces to find kingdoms. Edom's copper shows that a strong, organised society can leave few buildings. Some scholars call this the 'architectural bias', and it matters for how we judge David's kingdom too.
claims: Large-scale smelting at Khirbet en-Nahas and Timna in the 11th–9th centuries BC, dated by radiocarbon.
That this was run by an Edomite polity of largely nomadic people, and what that says about early kingdoms, is debated.
The Bible says David put garrisons in Edom (2 Samuel 8:14).

events.title: The temple: text and parallels
events.text: The Book of Kings describes Solomon's temple in detail: a porch, a great hall and an inner room, the Holy of Holies, where the Ark of the Covenant stood. No trace of it has been found, because the Temple Mount is a holy place and cannot be excavated. But temples of the same three-part plan are known, most closely at Ain Dara in Syria, and a small temple of this age was found at Tel Motza, just outside Jerusalem.
events.why: The Temple in Jerusalem became the centre of Jewish worship. After it was destroyed, prayer took its place: Jews still face Jerusalem when they pray, as Solomon asks in his dedication prayer.
claims: The building and dedication of the temple: 1 Kings 6–8.
Ain Dara has a three-part plan like the one described in 1 Kings 6.
Tel Motza: an Iron IIA temple with altar and courtyard, late 10th–early 9th century BC.
A stone shrine model from Khirbet Qeiyafa has a recessed doorframe that some compare with 1 Kings 6:31.
Facing Jerusalem in prayer, from 1 Kings 8.

events.title: Was there a united monarchy?
events.text: The Bible tells of one kingdom of all Israel under Saul, David and Solomon, which split in two after Solomon. Some historians, such as Israel Finkelstein, think the north and Judah were separate from the start, and that the 'united monarchy' is a later ideal. Others, such as Amihai Mazar, think a modest kingdom ruled from Jerusalem is the best reading of the evidence.
events.why: A 9th-century BC stele from Tel Dan names the 'House of David', so a dynasty named after David ruled Judah within about a century and a half. How large and how rich that kingdom was at the start is still open.
claims: One kingdom under David and Solomon, split after Solomon: 2 Samuel to 1 Kings 12.
The north and Judah were separate from the start; the united monarchy is a later ideal.
A modest united kingdom in the 10th century BC is the best reading of the evidence.
The Tel Dan stele names the 'House of David' (9th century BC).

events.title: The Mesha stele
events.text: About a century after the split, Mesha, king of Moab, set up a stone at Dibon boasting that he had thrown off the rule of Israel's king Omri and his son. It was found in 1868 and is now in the Louvre. In a broken line near the end, André Lemaire proposed reading 'House of David'. Others read a king's name, Balak, instead.
events.why: It is Moab's own side of a story the Bible tells too (2 Kings 3). If the reading is right, it is a second 9th-century witness to a dynasty named after David.
claims: Mesha of Moab's inscription from Dibon, naming Omri king of Israel.
Line 31 reads 'House of David': hypothetical but the most probable reading.
Line 31 cannot read 'House of David'; the name may be Balak.
